postTitle: Life Events and Your Finances: How to Plan Ahead
topic: Plan what you can see coming, buffer what you cannot

assumptions.notes: Emergency fund: a common guideline of three to six months of expenses (from the emergency fund post). No other figures. Illustrative.

buffers: An emergency fund, often 3 to 6 months of costs
A plan with slack in it
columnStory.disclosure: Illustrative. 3 to 6 months is a common guideline, not a rule.

hookVariants.narration: Most money shocks are not shocks. You knew they were coming.
There are two kinds of life event, and they call for different plans.
One question sorts every big money event: can you name roughly when it happens?

beats.narration: Petra can see some of hers years ahead. A child. A bigger home. A career break. A move abroad.
beats.subtext: A child, a home, a break, a move

beats.narration: Those can get a plan. Each one can go in a projection, with a rough date, a number and the bad case tested.
beats.subtext: A date, a number, the bad case

beats.narration: Others nobody can see coming. An illness. A redundancy. A family emergency. A market shock.
Those cannot be planned one by one. They usually get a buffer instead.
beats.subtext: Not a plan for each one

beats.narration: Three buffers do most of the work. An emergency fund, often three to six months of costs. Insurance that fits the household. And a plan with some slack in it.
A common mistake is mixing them up. Treating a planned baby as a surprise, or trying to predict every disaster.
beats.subtext: A planned baby is not a surprise

beats.narration: So one question sorts every event. Can you name roughly when it happens? Then it can go in the plan. If not, it usually gets a buffer.

cta.narration: Save this for your next five years.

caption.instagram:
Most money shocks are not shocks. You knew they were coming.

Some life events you can see years ahead: a child, a home, a career break, a move abroad. Those can get a plan: a rough date, a number, and the bad case tested. Others nobody sees coming: an illness, a redundancy, a family emergency, a market shock. Those usually get a buffer: an emergency fund (a common guideline is three to six months of costs), insurance that fits the household, and a plan with some slack.

The sorting question: can you name roughly when it happens? Then it can go in the plan. If not, it usually gets a buffer.
